862.title: Dirk Willems turns back
862.hook: fleeing across ice, he turns to rescue his pursuer who fell through, and is captured
862.howItsDone: Mennonite and Amish communities tell the story of Dirk Willems from the Martyrs Mirror, and an etching of him pulling his pursuer from the ice is a familiar image in Anabaptist homes and churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Menno Simons, the priest who joined the hunted. Your line was true faith cannot lie dormant. What did your faith, or your conscience, get up and do? Day eight hundred sixty-two.

The ice holds for the man running. It doesn't hold for the man chasing him. Winter, in a Dutch town called Asperen. A prisoner has just escaped, knotting strips of cloth into a rope and letting himself down from a window. He runs for the frozen water and starts across. Behind him comes the officer sent to catch him. The prisoner makes it over. Then he hears the crack, and the splash, and a man shouting for help from a hole in the ice. He's free. Nobody would blame him for running. The man in the water was coming to take him back to die. Today: Dirk Willems turns back.

Dirk's story comes to us through the Martyrs Mirror, a large book of Anabaptist martyr accounts. He had been arrested for his faith, the account says, for being baptized as a believer and letting others be baptized in his house. Tradition says prison food had left him thin, and that's why the ice held him. Then the pursuer fell through. And Dirk turned around, walked back out onto the ice he had just escaped across, and pulled the man out. Here's what happened next, and it's hard. The pursuer, the account says, wanted to let him go. But the town's burgomaster, standing on the bank, shouted at him to remember his oath. So the man Dirk had just saved took him back to prison. Dirk was condemned and burned. Why turn back? The accounts don't give a speech. But Anabaptists like Dirk read the Sermon on the Mount as instructions, not ideals. In the King James Bible, Jesus says: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." Paul puts it in plainer terms: "if thine enemy hunger, feed him." Dirk's enemy wasn't hungry. He was drowning. And Dirk had to decide, fast, whether those words were for real. In Mennonite and Amish communities his story is told and retold, and people in other churches, and in none, tell it too. It doesn't ask anyone to go looking for martyrdom. It asks a smaller and stranger question: when the one chasing you falls, what do you do?

Here's the practice: help someone chasing you. Bring to mind a person who's after you right now. Not in danger, just pressing. A boss with a deadline. A critic. A relative who keeps raising the same complaint. Someone you'd rather run from. Now ask what would help them. Not what would end the chase. What would help them. A finished task, a kind reply, a call back. Choose one small thing. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. If you don't, just hold them in mind without the usual defenses. The bell holds the time.
Dirk Willems. The Anabaptist who escaped across ice, then went back to save his drowning pursuer, and was captured for it.
Your line: he turned back. Today, when someone who's been hard on you stumbles, turn back toward them once, instead of walking on. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

863.title: Calvin in Geneva
863.hook: a shy French lawyer builds a church, schools and a refugee city
863.howItsDone: Reformed and Presbyterian churches trace their roots to Calvin's Geneva; their deacons and members often work with refugees and newcomers, and some congregations sponsor refugee families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dirk Willems on the ice, going back for the man chasing him. Your line was he turned back. Who did you turn back toward? Day eight hundred sixty-three.

One night's stop. That was the plan. A young Frenchman trained in law, who has had to leave his own country over his faith, is passing through Geneva on his way somewhere quiet, where he can read and write in peace. He describes himself, later, as shy by nature, someone who loved the shadows. But word gets around that he's in town, and an older preacher named William Farel comes to find him. Farel tells him to stay and help. The young man says no. Farel tells him that if he refuses, God will curse his quiet studies. The young man stays. His name is John Calvin. Today: Calvin in Geneva.
screen: `A SHY MAN WHO LOVED THE SHADOWS.`
`STAY, OR GOD WILL CURSE YOUR STUDIES.`

segments.voice: We know about that night because Calvin told it himself, in the preface to his commentary on the Psalms. He says Farel's words terrified him, as if God had reached down and stopped him on the road. And Geneva wasn't easy. The city threw him out once. Later it called him back, and he came. What he built there had three pieces. A church, organized with pastors, teachers, elders and deacons, the deacons charged with caring for the poor and the sick. Schools, so that children could read the Bible for themselves and young pastors could be trained. And a city of refuge. Calvin knew what it was to be a refugee, and Geneva became a place where people fleeing for their faith came, from France and from other lands, with funds set up to help the poor among them. The Bible gives that kind of welcome deep roots. In the King James wording of Leviticus: "the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Geneva in Calvin's time was also a strict and sometimes harsh place, and it put people on trial for their beliefs. Historians still weigh that part of the story, and it belongs in it. Churches in the Reformed and Presbyterian family trace themselves back to Geneva. And the shy man who wanted a quiet room spent the rest of his life in a busy, contested city full of strangers.
screen: `A CHURCH, WITH DEACONS FOR THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome a refugee. Let your shoulders drop. Then think of someone who had to leave home: a neighbor, a coworker, a family in the news, maybe someone in your own family tree. What did they have to leave behind? What would welcome look like for them this week? A meal. A donation to a group that helps new arrivals. Learning to say their name properly. Choose one. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Calvin. The refugee lawyer, pressed to stay in Geneva, who built a church, schools and a city that took in people fleeing for their faith.
Your line: a city of refuge. Today, make one corner of your life, your table, your desk, your conversation, a place where a stranger is welcome. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

864.title: Knowing God and ourselves
864.hook: Calvin's Institutes begin: true wisdom is knowing God and knowing ourselves
864.howItsDone: Reformed and Presbyterian Christians study Calvin's Institutes in seminaries and church study groups, and its opening on knowing God and ourselves is a familiar starting point for reflection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Calvin in Geneva, the shy refugee who stayed and built a place of welcome. Your line was a city of refuge. Where did you make room for a stranger? Day eight hundred sixty-four.

How do you open a book meant to explain the whole Christian faith? With God's attributes? With the creation of the world? With a proof? John Calvin wrote that kind of book, the Institutes of the Christian Religion, and he kept reworking it through his life. And the very first thing it says is not about God alone. In paraphrase: nearly all the wisdom we have, true and solid wisdom, comes down to two parts. Knowing God. And knowing ourselves. Two knowledges, braided together from the first sentence. Today: knowing God and ourselves.

Then Calvin admits something unexpected. The two are so tied together, he says, that it isn't easy to tell which one comes first. Look one way. When people take an honest look at themselves, they find need. Things they lack, wrongs they've done, limits they can't get past. And that very lack, Calvin says, sends them looking for God, the way an empty cup points to water. Now look the other way. He also says we never see ourselves clearly until we've first looked at God. Next to the light, we finally see our own shape. So it runs both directions. Self-knowledge pushes toward God. Knowledge of God shows us ourselves. Calvin didn't invent the pairing. It runs through the Psalms. One psalm asks, in the King James Bible: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" Another prays: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts." A person asking God to do the looking, because they can't fully see themselves. Paul says that for now we know in part, and one day "then shall I know even as also I am known." Calvin wrote in Latin, and the word he used for this knowledge was cognitio. In the Reformed tradition the Institutes is read as a foundational book. Other Christians, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, read him with different questions, and disagree with him on many things. But his opening move is one anyone can try: look honestly at yourself for a while, and notice where the looking leads.
screen: `NEXT TO THE LIGHT, OUR OWN SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: know one true thing about yourself. Sit quietly and let your breathing slow. Then ask yourself, gently, for one thing that's true about you right now. Not the most flattering thing. Not the harshest. Just true. Maybe something you need. Something you're carrying. Something you're good at and rarely admit. When it comes, don't argue with it. Just let it be known. If you pray, you can offer that one true thing to God, the way the psalm does: search me. If you don't, simply sit with it, honestly. The bell holds the time.
Cognitio. Calvin's Latin word for knowledge: the opening move of his Institutes, that knowing God and knowing ourselves lead into each other.
Your line: two knowledges. Today, when you learn something about yourself, even something small, notice where it points. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

865.title: John Knox
865.hook: a firebrand preacher shapes the Church of Scotland and its schools
865.howItsDone: The Church of Scotland and Presbyterian churches elsewhere trace their roots to the Scottish Reformation, in which Knox was a leading voice; they are governed by elders, and look back to the First Book of Discipline's plan for parish schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Calvin's word cognitio, knowledge: the first move of his Institutes, knowing God and knowing ourselves. Your line was two knowledges. What true thing did you learn about yourself, and where did it point? Day eight hundred sixty-five.

A man chained to an oar. He's Scottish, a priest turned Protestant preacher, and he's been captured when the castle where he was preaching fell to a French force. Now he's rowing on a French galley, a prisoner, pulling the same heavy oar day after day. He doesn't know if he'll ever see Scotland again. He does. And when he comes home, years later, he preaches so fiercely that crowds pour out of the church and into the streets. His name is John Knox, and he left Scotland a church and an idea about schools that outlasted his anger. Today: John Knox.
screen: `A CHURCH, AND AN IDEA ABOUT SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: Knox was a firebrand, and there's no softening it. After the galleys he spent time in exile, including in Calvin's Geneva, and came back to Scotland convinced the church needed rebuilding from the ground. His preaching stirred crowds, and some of them tore apart altars and images in the churches. He wrote a furious pamphlet against women rulers. He argued face to face with Mary, Queen of Scots, a Catholic queen, and the meetings are remembered as storms. For Scotland's Catholics, the change he led meant losing their Mass and their churches, and that loss is part of the story too. But here's the piece that's quieter. When Knox and his fellow ministers set out a plan for the new church, the First Book of Discipline, they wrote about schools. Their plan called for a schoolmaster in every parish, so that children could learn to read, the poor as well as the rich, with colleges in the larger towns and the universities above them. Part of the reason was simple: if every Christian should read the Bible, every child needs to be able to read. That's an old idea in a new place. In the King James Bible, Moses tells the people to teach God's words "diligently unto thy children" and to talk of them "when thou sittest in thine house." Knox's plan put that at the scale of a whole country. It wasn't all built at once, and the money was fought over. But the idea took root. The Church of Scotland grew from this time, and in the generations after Knox it settled into a Presbyterian church, run by elders rather than bishops. So did the picture of a schoolhouse beside every church.

Here's the practice: learn something from Scotland. Take the one big idea from this story: every child should be able to read. Then ask yourself who taught you. A parent with a picture book. A first-grade teacher. A librarian. A sibling. Hold that person in mind for a while. Then think of someone who's still learning, a child, a new reader, someone learning a new language, and one small way you could help. If you pray, you can give thanks for your teachers. If you don't, simply remember them with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
John Knox. A fierce Scottish preacher who helped shape the Church of Scotland, and whose plan called for a school in every parish.
Your line: a school in every parish. Today, teach someone one small thing you know, or let someone teach you. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

866.title: Tyndale's last prayer (1536)
866.hook: strangled and burned, he prays: Lord, open the king of England's eyes
866.howItsDone: Christians in different churches pray for those in authority, often in set prayers during services; Tyndale is remembered as a translator and martyr, and some churches mark his day in their calendars.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Knox, the firebrand who planned schools for Scotland. Your line was a school in every parish. What did you teach, or learn? Day eight hundred sixty-six.

A dinner argument in an English manor house. A young scholar named William Tyndale is debating a learned man, and the man says something that makes Tyndale lose patience. According to John Foxe, who told the story in his book of martyrs, Tyndale shot back that if God spared his life, he would make a boy who drives the plow know more of the scripture than he did. Erasmus had wished for a farmer singing scripture at the plow. Tyndale spent the rest of his life trying to make that wish real, and it cost him that life. Today: Tyndale's last prayer.

Tyndale wanted an English Bible translated straight from the Greek and Hebrew, in words a farmhand could follow. In England he couldn't get permission. So he left, and worked abroad, moving from city to city. His New Testament in English was printed on the continent and smuggled into England, hidden among goods. Church authorities there bought up copies and burned them. Tyndale kept translating, and kept revising. Then a man who had befriended him betrayed him. He was arrested, held in a prison castle near Brussels, tried as a heretic and condemned. Foxe tells how it ended: Tyndale was tied to the stake, strangled, and his body burned. And before he died, Foxe says, he cried out with a loud voice: Lord, open the king of England's eyes. Here's what stands out in that prayer. It isn't a curse. It isn't revenge. The king whose bishops had burned his books is the one he prays for. And what he asks for is sight. That echoes the first letter to Timothy, written in Paul's name, which says in the King James Bible that prayers should be made "For kings, and for all that are in authority." Some readers see an answer in what came after: English Bibles allowed in English churches, by the king's own permission, with Tyndale's wording carried into them. Some hear his phrasing in later English Bibles too, the King James among them. The last thing he's remembered saying asks for a leader to see clearly.

Here's the practice: pray for a leader's eyes. Take one slow breath. Then picture someone with power over your life or your world. A president, a governor, a mayor. A boss. A principal. Maybe someone you strongly disagree with. Notice whatever comes up when you think of them, and let it pass. Then, instead of an accusation, ask for sight: that they might see clearly. If you pray, you can borrow Tyndale's words, changed a little: Lord, open their eyes, or the line from Timothy about kings and all in authority. If you don't, simply hold them in mind without wishing them harm. The bell holds the time.
Tyndale. The English translator who, dying at the stake, is remembered crying out: Lord, open the king of England's eyes.
Your line: open the king's eyes. Today, when you hear news about a leader you oppose, pause before the criticism and wish them clear sight first. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

867.title: Henry's break
867.hook: a king's divorce, a split from Rome, and monasteries dissolved
867.howItsDone: Anglicans tell the story of their church through the English Reformation, Henry's break among it, while Catholics remember the same years as a break from Rome and a loss; the ruins of old abbeys are still visited, and in some, prayers are said again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tyndale's last prayer: at the stake, he asked God to open the king of England's eyes. Your line was open the king's eyes. Whose eyes did you pray for, or hope for? Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

A king wants a son. That's where today's story starts, and it ends with empty monasteries all over the English countryside. Henry the Eighth is married to Catherine of Aragon. Before that, she was married to his older brother, Arthur, until Arthur died. Henry and Catherine have a daughter, Mary, but no son who lives. Henry becomes convinced that the marriage was wrong from the very beginning, and he asks the pope to declare that it never truly existed. The pope does not give him the answer he wants. So Henry stops asking. Today: Henry's break.
screen: `HE ASKS THE POPE TO END HIS MARRIAGE.`

segments.voice: Henry built his case on a verse. Leviticus says, in the King James Bible, "if a man shall take his brother's wife, it is an unclean thing", and it adds that such a couple will be childless. Henry read his own life in that line. His opponents pointed to Deuteronomy, which tells a man to marry his brother's widow if the brother died without children. Same Bible, two answers, and a crown hanging between them. When Rome would not grant what he asked, Henry and his Parliament cut the ties instead. Henry married Anne Boleyn in secret, and Thomas Cranmer, the new archbishop of Canterbury, declared the marriage to Catherine void. Then new laws named the king supreme head of the church in England. Then came the monasteries. Royal commissioners visited the abbeys and priories and reported on them, and one by one they were closed. Their lands went to the crown, and much of it was sold on to wealthy families. Monks and nuns who had given their lives to those houses were sent out of them. Some got pensions. Some became parish priests. Some had nowhere obvious to go. Roofs were stripped for their lead, and walls became quarries. Here's the strange part. Henry did not think of himself as a Protestant. He kept the Mass. The break was first about authority: who rules the church in England. Christians remember it differently. Anglicans trace their church's own story through these years, though much of what shaped it came later. Catholics remember the break as a wound, and the closing of the monasteries as a loss. Faith and politics are knotted so tightly here that it's hard to pull them apart. Jesus, asked about paying taxes to Caesar, said: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's." The hard question in Henry's England was who got to decide which was which.
screen: `THE KING AS HEAD OF THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the people who lost their homes. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a monk or a nun walking out through an abbey gate for the last time, leaving a place they had meant to stay in for life. You don't need their names. Let them walk slowly. Then widen the picture: anyone today who has lost a home because of decisions made far above them. If you pray, you can pray for them, the ones from long ago and the ones now. If you don't, just keep them company in your mind for a while. The bell holds the time.
Henry's break. A king's quarrel over a marriage that became a split between the church in England and Rome, and the closing of England's monasteries.
Your line: politics and faith. Today, when you see faith pulled into a political fight, ask one quiet question: who pays the price? Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

868.title: The Book of Common Prayer (1549)
868.hook: Cranmer puts worship in English, prayers still used worldwide
868.carry: cleanse the thoughts of our hearts
868.howItsDone: Anglicans and Episcopalians pray from prayer books descended from Cranmer's, and in their churches the communion service often begins with the collect for purity, said by the priest or by everyone together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Henry's break: a marriage, a split from Rome, and monasteries emptied. Your line was politics and faith. Where did you see the two tangled, and who paid? Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

"Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God." "Till death us do part." "Earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust." Lines like these turn up at weddings and gravesides, in novels and in films, and the people saying them don't always know where they came from. They come from one book, made by the archbishop from yesterday's story, Thomas Cranmer. Henry broke with Rome, but in the parish churches the services were still said in Latin. Cranmer wanted something else: the whole service in English, said out loud, in a book everyone shared. Today: Common Prayer.
screen: `DEARLY BELOVED. TILL DEATH US DO PART.`

segments.voice: Common here doesn't mean ordinary. It means shared. One book, for every parish, so the priest and the people pray the same words in the same language. Cranmer didn't write most of it from nothing. He was a translator at heart. He took old Latin prayers and turned them into English with a rhythm that is easy to say together. Here's one. Before the book, a short Latin prayer was said quietly by the priest as he got ready for Mass. Cranmer moved it to the opening of the communion service, put it in English, and had it said aloud. In the prayer book's later revision it reads: "Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid: Cleanse the thoughts of our hearts by the inspiration of thy Holy Spirit, that we may perfectly love thee, and worthily magnify thy holy Name; through Christ our Lord. Amen." A prayer of this shape is called a collect: who God is, what we ask, and why. Notice what it asks to have cleaned. Not hands. Not deeds. Thoughts. It sounds like the psalm: "Create in me a clean heart, O God." Not everyone wanted the new book. In the west of England, some people rose up against the English service and asked for the old Latin one back. Under Queen Mary it was set aside, and later it returned, revised. Anglican churches in different countries still pray in words that come down from it, and the collect for purity is still said at the start of communion in Anglican churches and others. The book that began in an argument became a set of words people say together.
screen: `CLEANSE THE THOUGHTS, NOT JUST THE HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the collect for purity. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can say it slowly, a line at a time, with a breath between: Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open. All desires known. From whom no secrets are hid.
